blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Objective: Multimodal survival prediction jointly analyzes histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs), genomic profiles, and clinical variables to stratify patients by risk. However, existing approaches often inadequately account for granularity differences across modalities, particularly in spatial organization and feature dimensionality. To address these challenges, we propose HGASurv, which introduces a hierarchical WSI encoding module and a clinical-guided graph propagation module for granularity-aware multimodal integration. Methods: The hierarchical WSI encoding module maps WSI patch features onto a spatial grid using their original coordinates and applies parallel convolutions to construct representations at patch, local-neighborhood, and regional scales. Genomic signature embeddings then query these scale-specific WSI representations through cross-modal co-attention, producing signature-conditioned morphological features. The clinical-guided graph propagation module uses clinical variables to define patient-similarity edges and propagates fused image-genomic node embeddings with graph attention, integrating clinical information through topology rather than feature concatenation. Results: Across three TCGA cohorts, HGASurv achieved the strongest overall C-index performance, with ablation studies supporting the complementary contributions of the hierarchical WSI encoding and clinical-guided graph propagation modules. Conclusion and Significance: By introducing hierarchical WSI encoding and clinical-guided graph propagation, HGASurv unifies multi-scale pathology representation with topology-based clinical integration in a hierarchical granularity-aware framework. This design shows that matching representation and integration mechanisms to modality-specific granularity improves multimodal survival prediction.

blocks.en: I Introduction
blocks.zh: 一. 导言

blocks.en:
Survival analysis is a fundamental statistical framework in prognostic
research by accommodating censored data to simultaneously model the timing and occurrence
of clinical events [ 1 , 2 ] . By stratifying patients into risk groups and
estimating survival probabilities over the follow-up period, survival prediction supports
treatment planning and informs patients about the likely course of disease [ 3 ] . Driven by recent advances in deep learning, researchers have shifted
their focus from single-modality analysis to integrating richer multimodal information,
thus achieving superior prognostic performance [ 4 ] . Histopathological
whole-slide images (WSIs) provide spatial information about tissue morphology and
architecture; genomic sequencing profiles describe the molecular state; and clinical
variables summarize patient- and disease-level status. However, these diverse modalities
associated with patient survival outcomes exhibit substantial heterogeneity in information
granularity, particularly in spatial organization and feature dimensionality. Tissue
morphology in histopathological WSIs is spatially organized across multiple scales, and a
single WSI can measure up to 100,000 × 100,000 100{,}000\times 100{,}000 pixels [ 5 ] . Genomic
profiles may contain tens of thousands of variables, whereas clinical data typically
comprise fewer than 100 variables. Such profound heterogeneity in information granularity
renders the integration of multimodal data for survival prediction highly challenging,
thereby demanding tailored model architectures.

blocks.en:
A series of deep learning-based models has emerged for multimodal data fusion in survival
prediction. Most existing approaches, such as MCAT [ 6 ] , SurvPath [ 5 ] ,
SurMoE [ 7 ] and DeReF [ 8 ] , focus on
integrating histopathological images with genomic profiles, while several works such as
PG-TFNet [ 9 ] and SAMMS [ 10 ] further integrate clinical variables as an
additional modality.
Although existing models have demonstrated promising performance
in survival prediction, certain key challenges still remain unaddressed. On the one hand,
regarding large-scale histopathological images, the prevailing paradigm involves dividing
WSIs into small patches and extracting patch-level visual representations for downstream
fusion. Aggregating these patch-level features without preserving their spatial
arrangement can obscure the global tissue architecture, thereby hindering the model from
discerning pathological morphological patterns. On the other hand, regarding the fusion of
low-dimensional clinical variables, existing methods generally concatenate clinical
variables with high-dimensional features learned from other modalities before the final
survival head. Considering the substantial dimensionality disparity, this concatenation
strategy risks rendering clinical variables diluted or suppressed by dominant visual and
genomic features, which can limit their contribution to survival prediction.

To address the above issues, we propose a H ierarchical G ranularity- A ware integration framework for multimodal Surv ival
prediction ( HGASurv ).
To preserve WSI spatial organization, HGASurv
introduces a hierarchical WSI encoding module. Patch embeddings are arranged on a spatial
grid according to their original coordinates and processed by parallel convolutions to
derive representations at patch, local-neighborhood, and regional scales. Following the
genomic-signature grouping in MCAT [ 6 ] , six signature embeddings query each
scale-specific WSI representation through cross-modal co-attention. The resulting
pathology and genomic representations are fused into an image–genomic embedding. To
incorporate clinical variables without direct feature concatenation, HGASurv introduces a
clinical-guided graph propagation module. Clinical similarity defines an undirected
patient graph, over which a graph attention network propagates the fused image–genomic
embeddings. Clinical variables thus influence prediction through graph topology rather
than being appended to the image–genomic node features. Together, these components form a
hierarchy from intramodal multi-scale WSI encoding, through within-patient
pathology–genomics fusion, to clinically guided inter-patient propagation. This hierarchy
aligns each representation and integration mechanism with the information granularity of
the corresponding modality. Our code is available at https://github.com/PeikerYu/HGASurv . The main contributions of our work are as
follows. • We introduce a hierarchical WSI encoding module that reconstructs patch
embeddings on a spatial grid and derives multi-scale pathology representations at patch,
local-neighborhood, and regional scales. • We introduce a clinical-guided graph propagation module that uses clinical
variables to define patient-similarity topology and propagates fused image–genomic
embeddings with graph attention, integrating clinical information through topology
rather than feature concatenation. • We evaluate HGASurv on TCGA-GBMLGG, TCGA-BLCA, and TCGA-UCEC, achieving
C-indices of 0.854 ± 0.023 0.854\pm 0.023 , 0.692 ± 0.032 0.692\pm 0.032 , and 0.721 ± 0.098 0.721\pm 0.098 , respectively
(mean ± \pm SD over five folds), and the strongest overall C-index performance across
the three cohorts. Ablation studies support the complementary contributions of the
hierarchical WSI encoding and clinical-guided graph propagation modules.

blocks.en: II Related Work
blocks.zh: 二. 相关工作

blocks.en: II-A Survival Prediction
blocks.zh: 二-生存预测

blocks.en:
Classical survival prediction commonly relies on the Cox proportional hazards
model [ 2 ] and its penalized variants [ 11 ] , which relate covariates to
risk under the proportional-hazards assumption. Random Survival Forests [ 12 ] capture nonlinear effects nonparametrically. Neural models extend these foundations:
DeepSurv [ 13 ] replaces the Cox linear predictor with a multilayer perceptron
(MLP), whereas DeepHit [ 14 ] directly models discrete-time event distributions
without the proportional-hazards assumption. Dynamic-DeepHit further handles longitudinal
data with competing risks [ 15 ] . Although effective for structured covariates,
these methods are primarily unimodal and do not explicitly model interactions among
pathology, genomics, and clinical variables.

blocks.en: II-B Pathology–Genomics Multimodal Survival Prediction
blocks.zh: II-B 病理学 - 基因组学

blocks.en:
Existing pathology–genomics survival methods explore different strategies for
integrating histological and genomic information. MCAT [ 6 ] allows functional
genomic-signature embeddings to query histology features, whereas
SurvPath [ 5 ] models dense interactions between biological-pathway and
histology-patch tokens. MOTCat [ 16 ] uses optimal transport to align histology
patches with genomic embeddings under global structure consistency.
SurMoE [ 7 ] employs dynamic expert routing to balance heterogeneous
inputs, while DeReF [ 8 ] decouples shared, specific, and exclusive features
before reorganizing them for MoE fusion. Liu et al. [ 17 ] investigate
view-aware collaborative learning for joint survival prediction and subgroup
identification. However, these methods primarily focus on cross-modal interaction or
alignment, while explicit modeling of WSI spatial organization across multiple
morphological scales remains less explored.

blocks.zh: II-C 临床融合和病人关系模型

blocks.en:
Compared with pathology and genomic data, structured clinical variables have received
less attention as a distinct modality in multimodal survival models.
PG-TFNet [ 9 ] and SAMMS [ 10 ] concatenate clinical variables with
learned pathology–genomics representations before the survival head.
ModalTune [ 18 ] instead uses a lightweight Modal Adapter to
inject auxiliary modalities into a frozen slide-level foundation model. Sucre et
al. [ 19 ] compare early fusion with predictor-level late fusion, with the
latter combining outputs from independently trained unimodal models.
SurvPGC [ 20 ] encodes clinical information as text embeddings and fuses
them with pathology and genomic representations through cross-attention. These approaches integrate clinical information within individual patients rather than using clinical similarity to guide cross-patient information exchange.

blocks.en: IV-B Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods

blocks.en:
To benchmark HGASurv against state-of-the-art survival prediction methods, Table I compares it with 19 baselines across the GBMLGG, BLCA, and UCEC cohorts. These methods use pathology images, genomic profiles, clinical variables, or their combinations.
The genomic-only baselines comprise SNN [ 28 ] and its self-attention-enhanced variant SNNTrans. The pathology-only group includes attention-based MIL methods (AttnMIL [ 30 ] , DeepAttnMISL [ 33 ] , CLAM-SB, and CLAM-MB [ 24 ] ), Transformer-based aggregation (TransMIL [ 34 ] ), and feature distillation (DTFD-MIL [ 35 ] ).

唯基因组基线包括SNN [28] 及其自觉增强的变体SNNTrans. 病理类只包括基于注意力的MIL方法(AttnMIL [30],DeepAttnMISL [33],CLAM-SB,和CLAM-MB [24]),基于变形器的聚合(TransMIL [34]),以及特征蒸馏(DTFD-MIL [35]).

blocks.en: The pathology–genomics baselines span three fusion strategies: feature-level integration with Pathomic Fusion [ 36 ] , PORPOISE [ 37 ] , and PG-MLIF [ 40 ] ; cross-modal interaction and alignment with MCAT [ 6 ] , MOTCat [ 16 ] , CMTA [ 38 ] , and MGCT [ 39 ] ; and adaptive expert fusion with DeReF [ 8 ] and SurMoE [ 7 ] . The trimodal baselines include the prediction-level late-fusion approach of Sucre et al. [ 19 ] and the clinical-text-based cross-modal integration of SurvPGC [ 20 ] .

blocks.en: The best multimodal result exceeds the best unimodal result in each cohort. However, the trimodal baselines outperform the strongest pathology–genomics baseline on UCEC but not on GBMLGG or BLCA, suggesting that adding clinical information does not guarantee consistent improvements across integration strategies and cohorts.
blocks.zh: 最好的多式联运结果超过了每一组中最好的单一模式结果。 然而,三模式基线比UCEC上最强的病理学-基因组基线要好,但GBMLGG或BLCA上则不然,这表明,增加临床信息并不能保证在一体化战略和组别上取得一致的改进。

HGASurv combines within-patient pathology–genomics interactions with clinically defined relationships between patients; the component and clinical-integration ablations in Tables II and III further examine the contributions of these design elements. The out-of-fold risk predictions stratify patients into groups with significantly different survival outcomes across all three cohorts as Fig. 2 shows.

blocks.en: IV-C 1 Component Ablation
blocks.zh: 四-C 1 构成部分

blocks.en: To isolate the individual and joint contributions of hierarchical WSI encoding and clinical-guided graph propagation, Table II compares the full HGASurv model with three variants that remove graph propagation, replace hierarchical WSI encoding with the single 1 × 1 1\times 1 pathology branch, or apply both changes.
blocks.zh: 为了隔离分级WSI编码和临床导图传播的个人贡献和联合贡献,表二将全HGASurv模型与三个变体进行比较,这些变体去除图传播,将分级WSI编码替换为单1×1乘1的病理学分支,或者应用两种变体.

blocks.en: TABLE II: Component ablation of HGASurv across three TCGA cohorts.
blocks.zh: 表格 二:HGASurv的组件跨越三个TCGA组群.

blocks.en: Removing either hierarchical WSI encoding or clinical-guided graph propagation reduces the mean C-index across all three cohorts (Table II ). The ablated variants fall below the strongest pathology–genomics baseline in each cohort (Table I ), whereas full HGASurv outperforms these baselines. Removing both components further degrades performance on GBMLGG and UCEC. These findings indicate that the two components provide complementary benefits and are key contributors to HGASurv’s performance advantage over pathology–genomics baselines.
blocks.zh: 消除分级WSI编码或临床指导图表的传播,可减少所有三个组别的平均C指数(表二)。 衰减的变体低于每个组群中最强的病理-基因组基线(表一),而完整的HGASurv则超过了这些基线。 删除这两个组件会进一步降低GBMLGG和UCEC上的性能. 这些调查结果表明,这两个组成部分提供了互补的好处,是HGASurv相对于病理基因组基线的性能优势的主要贡献者。

blocks.en: IV-C 2 Clinical Integration Strategies
blocks.zh: IV-C 2 临床融合战略

blocks.en: To assess whether clinical variables improve survival prediction and how they should be incorporated, Table III compares three configurations while keeping the image–genomic encoder, patient splits, and training and evaluation protocols fixed. First, the No clinical variables configuration predicts survival directly from the image–genomic embedding without clinical inputs or graph propagation. Second, Clinical feature concatenation combines encoded clinical variables with the image–genomic embedding before the MLP survival head. Third, the proposed Clinical-guided graph propagation configuration uses clinical variables to construct a patient graph and propagates image–genomic embeddings between clinically similar patients before survival prediction.

blocks.en: To assess the contribution of clinically informed patient connectivity, Table IV compares three graph topologies. The Self-loop graph retains the GAT and survival head with only self-connections to evaluate graph processing without cross-patient information exchange. The Random graph uses Chung–Lu sampling [ 43 ] based on the clinical graph’s node degrees to test whether arbitrary patient connections yield comparable benefits. blocks.en: V Conclusion
blocks.zh: 五 结论

blocks.en:
We presented HGASurv, a multimodal survival prediction framework that represents and
integrates pathology, genomics, and clinical variables according to their information
granularity. Within pathology, patch features retain their spatial arrangement and are
encoded at patch, local-neighborhood, and regional scales; across modalities,
low-dimensional clinical variables shape predictions through the connectivity of a
patient-similarity graph rather than competing with high-dimensional image–genomic
embeddings as concatenated features. On three TCGA cohorts, HGASurv achieved the strongest
overall C-index performance among the evaluated methods, and component ablations supported
the complementary contributions of hierarchical WSI encoding and graph-based clinical
integration. Moreover, graph-based clinical integration outperformed direct concatenation
of the same clinical variables in all three cohorts.

颗粒性。 在病理学中,补丁特征保持其空间安排,并且
以补丁、本地邻居和区域尺度编码;
低维临床变量的形状预测,通过连接
与高维图像 - 基因组比对
嵌入为凸化特征. 在三个TCGA组中,HGASurv取得了最强的成绩.
所评价方法的C-指数总体业绩以及支助的组成部分

融入社会。 此外,基于图表的临床结合表现超过了直接结合
所有三个组的相同临床变量。

blocks.en:
Although these results suggest a benefit of tailoring representation and integration
to modality-specific information granularity, further investigation is needed to establish
how far this benefit extends beyond the present evaluation and how it arises in individual
predictions. Future work will evaluate HGASurv in cohorts independent of TCGA and assess
its sensitivity to feature-extraction and graph-construction choices. Patient-level
analyses will investigate how scale-specific pathology representations and information
exchanged through clinical neighborhoods shape individual predictions.
